newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan puts squeeze on unapproved China investment.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan puts squeeze on unapproved China investment.

text.p: Taiwan on Wednesday urged local firms to stop making unauthorised investments in rival China and vowed to ferret out and punish illegal projects despite evidence that Beijing was helping them to keep a low profile.

The Securities and Exchange Commission, the market watchdog, put teeth into the crackdown by vowing stricter screening of rights issues and stock market listings -- aiming to keep violators out of Taiwan's lucrative home markets.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, was not expected to make it easy to track down unauthorised investments.
Taiwan's Commercial Times said Beijing had taken notice of Taipei's caution and ordered agencies to keep Taiwan investments confidential to ensure a huge investment flow does not dry up.
Taiwan bans direct investments in China, but some US$30 billion in authorised "indirect" investment has flowed into the mainland under a political thaw begun in the late 1908s.
Banking sector and big infrastructural investments such as steel and power plants remain explicitly banned. In 1996, two major Taiwan firms cancelled power plant projects under pressure from Taipei.

The economics ministry said China projects must not begin without authorisation from its Investment Commission and said all Taiwan agencies would focus on suspected investors' fund flows, tax payments and "any illegal matters".
"We call on Taiwan firms investing in China to stop investments as soon as possible before they gain approval," the commission said in a statement.
Authorities can impose fines, repeatedly if necessary, of T$3 million to T$15 million (US$110,000-US$550,000), it said.

Some analysts have said the crackdown, which aims to keep Taiwan from growing dangerously dependent on the economy of its main adversary, could backfire if Taiwan investors determined to make China investments simply moved their financing offshore.
Banking investments appeared to be a particular concern.
On March 12, just a day after a visiting mainland official confirmed that Taiwan interests were financing a Shanghai bank, the commission warned local firms not to set up banks in China.

Di Weiping, a Shanghai-based vice president of China's central bank, had said that Beijing had approved a Taiwan firm's application to set up the first Taiwan-invested bank in Shanghai -- First Sino Bank.
What is more, Di said another unidentified Taiwan group had applied to succeed First Sino's US$80 million investment and set up a second Taiwan-funded bank in Shanghai.
Di declined to identify either project's backers.

Taiwan media have named First Sino's backer as Pou Chen Corp , a major investor in mainland footwear, saying Pou Chen owner Tsai Chi-chien and his brother Tsai Nan-feng applied as private individuals.
The Tsais have been unavailable for comment and Pou Chen executives refused to discuss the issue.
Many Taiwan investments in China are known to have been routed through offshore subsidiaries or through individuals with foreign nationalities to avoid Taiwan's screening process.
The watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission said such evasive measures were clear violations.

"If any companies' board directors or major shareholders violate the rules to launch illegal investments in China, our commission will see them as breaking the honesty and integrity principle," a commission spokeswoman told Reuters.
"And we likely will adopt stricter screening on their applications for rights issue and listings," she said.
Pou Chen shares plunged 5.5 percent on Wednesday as word of the crackdown swept the market.
